c.tagline: Australia's sun-soaked western capital of river, beaches, and endless blue sky.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed cabs (Swan Taxis, Black & White) are metered; you can hail on the street, wait at ranks, or book via the 13cabs/Swan apps. Uber, Ola, and DiDi are widely available and often cheaper.

emergency.note: 000 is Australia's national emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 112 also works from mobiles and 106 is the text-based line for the deaf.

hood_desc: The compact riverside downtown around Elizabeth Quay, St Georges Terrace, and the Hay Street and Murray Street malls, with the city's main shopping, dining, and free CAT bus loops; best for first-timers who want to be central and walk or ride to everything.

Perth's buzziest nightlife and dining quarter just north of the railway, packed with bars, live-music venues, and multicultural restaurants alongside the Perth Cultural Centre (WA Museum Boola Bardip and the Art Gallery of WA); suits night owls and foodies.

The historic port city ('Freo') at the mouth of the Swan River, full of heritage limestone buildings, the weekend Fremantle Markets, craft breweries, and a bohemian arts scene; a favorite for its relaxed, characterful vibe.

A leafy, upmarket inner suburb ('Subi') with tree-lined streets, cafe and boutique strips along Rokeby and Hay Streets, and a village feel; suits travelers wanting a calm, stylish residential base a few minutes from the CBD.
A laid-back Indian Ocean beach suburb with a wide white-sand beach, an oceanfront pool and skate park, and casual beachfront bars and eateries; best for sun, surf, and sunset seekers.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Trains and buses run roughly 5:30am to midnight (later on Fridays and weekends), with trains about every 10-15 minutes on the busiest lines; late-night service is limited, so ride apps or taxis cover the small hours.
transit.note: Four free CAT (Central Area Transit) bus loops circle the Perth CBD and Fremantle, and travel within the CBD Free Transit Zone - including trains between City West and Claisebrook - is free for everyone.
transit.pay: Tap a SmartRider smartcard (buy and top up at stations, newsagents, and machines) on the readers when boarding and alighting, or pay cash to the driver or at ticket machines. From January 2026 Transperth moved to a simplified flat-rate fare; SmartRider saves roughly 10-30% over cash, everyone travels free on Sundays, and the four CAT bus loops and the CBD Free Transit Zone are always free.

tip.r: Not expected - hospitality staff earn a full wage. Rounding up the bill or leaving around 10% for great service is appreciated but never obligatory.

landmarks: Elizabeth Quay
A striking waterfront precinct on the Swan River with a sculptural pedestrian bridge and skyline views that anchor Perth's modern image.
Kings Park and Botanic Garden
One of the world's largest inner-city parks, prized for its Instagram-famous purple jacaranda blooms and skyline lookout points.
Bell Tower (Swan Bells)
A distinctive glass-and-copper spire on the Swan River housing historic bells, including some from London's St Martin-in-the-Fields.
Cottesloe Beach
Perth's most photographed beach, famous for its Norfolk pines, turquoise water, and postcard sunsets over the Indian Ocean.
Fremantle Prison
A UNESCO World Heritage-listed former colonial prison whose imposing limestone walls make for an atmospheric historical visit.
Perth Mint
Australia's oldest operating mint, where visitors can view the world's largest gold coin and watch a live gold pour.
Rottnest Island
A short ferry ride from Perth, famous for its pristine bays and the endearing quokka, star of countless "quokka selfies."
Crawley Edge Boatshed (Blue Boat House)
A tiny, vividly blue boatshed on the Swan River that has become one of Perth's most-photographed and Instagrammed landmarks.
South Perth Foreshore
The classic vantage point across the Swan River for capturing Perth's glittering CBD skyline, especially at sunset.
Fremantle Round House
Western Australia's oldest surviving public building, a striking 12-sided limestone fort overlooking the harbor entrance.

train.note: Australia has no international railways, so all services from Perth are domestic. The Indian Pacific crosses 4,352 km to Adelaide and Sydney via the Nullarbor, taking about four days with two nights of desert running; it leaves from the East Perth Terminal and is an all-inclusive tourist train that sells out months ahead. Everyday regional travel is with Transwa, whose Prospector reaches Kalgoorlie in around 7 hours from East Perth, the Australind runs to Bunbury, and the AvonLink and MerredinLink serve the Wheatbelt. Transperth's suburban network, including the airport line, covers Fremantle, Joondalup and Mandurah from Perth Underground and Perth stations.

bus.note: No international coaches operate in Australia, and no scheduled coach crosses the Nullarbor between Perth and the eastern states, so the Indian Pacific or a flight is the alternative. Transwa (https://www.transwa.wa.gov.au/) is the main regional coach network, linking over 240 destinations from the East Perth Terminal and the Elizabeth Quay bus station to the South West, Esperance, Albany and Geraldton. Integrity Coach Lines runs the long north-west routes up to Exmouth, Karratha and Broome, a journey of well over 30 hours. Book Transwa online or by phone; some remote services run only a few times a week.

ferry.note: Perth has no international or interstate passenger ferries; the only sea crossing is the 19 km hop to Rottnest Island, which around 330,000 people a year make. From B Shed in Fremantle the crossing is about 25-30 minutes, from Barrack Street Jetty in the Perth CBD around 90 minutes including the river run, and from Hillarys roughly 45 minutes. Services run year-round but are busiest and priciest over summer and school holidays, so book ahead; bikes and luggage are carried for a fee. Transperth also runs a short commuter ferry across the Swan River between Elizabeth Quay and Mends Street in South Perth.
